extracted.intended_audience: educated general readers interested in moral/philosophical essays (readers of Montaigne)
extracted.subtask_description: A translated excerpt from Montaigne's Essays giving moral and practical reflections on human nature, virtue, rulership, idleness, communication, and behavior. The page is not a formal rubric but contains many normative claims and prescriptive observations about conduct and judgement.

rubrics_metrics.name: Melancholy contains a mixture of pleasure
rubrics_metrics.description: In sorrow there is some mixture of pleasure; there is design, consent, and complacency in giving oneself up to melancholy. Some constitutions feed upon it.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Montaigne cites poets and painters (e.g., 'Est quaedam flere voluptas') and notes that facial expressions for weeping and laughter overlap; extremes of laughter may bring tears. This is used to explain why people may consciously or unconsciously embrace melancholy.

rubrics_metrics.name: Virtue is mixed with vice
rubrics_metrics.description: Even our best virtues contain a tincture of vice; human moral qualities are 'patch and motley.'
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Montaigne argues that even Plato's purest virtue would reveal some human mixture upon introspection. He adduces the claim (via Tacitus) that laws of justice themselves cannot subsist without some mixture of injustice for public utility. The guidance is a caution against expecting absolute moral purity in oneself or institutions.

rubrics_metrics.name: Excessive intellectual perspicacity is impractical
rubrics_metrics.description: Too much subtlety and curiosity (penetrating light) makes minds unfit for practical business; we must blunt and veil intellects to adapt them to earthly life.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Montaigne observes that less speculative souls are more successful in managing affairs; over-analysis hinders election and action. Example: Simonides, who, given too many subtle considerations, despaired of deciding. Practical managers often cannot fully explain how they succeed; verbosity and deep inquiry can impede effective action.

rubrics_metrics.name: Prefer action and manageable instruments to exhaustive inquiry
rubrics_metrics.description: A little engine well handled is sufficient for executions; the best managers often cannot account for their success, while the greatest talkers often achieve nothing to purpose.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Illustrated by anecdotes of eloquent advisers who mismanaged large revenues when tested; Montaigne endorses pragmatic, hands-on competence over theoretical perfection or rhetorical display.

rubrics_metrics.name: Rulers must remain active and show personal engagement
rubrics_metrics.description: An emperor (or prince) should continue to govern and show presence even in sickness; 'An emperor must die standing.' Rulers devoted to ease disgust subjects and undermine willingness to serve.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Examples: Vespasian, Adrian, Ottoman princes, Soliman, Edward III. Montaigne argues that military and executive office is not an ease; presence on the spot and active direction (especially in war) confer honour and legitimacy. Delegation that entirely removes the ruler from danger or labor degrades the office.

rubrics_metrics.name: Stoic discipline: restrict bodily needs to serve honourable ends
rubrics_metrics.description: A philosopher and brave man ought to allow the body only what is necessary, keeping soul and body intent and busy about honourable, great, and virtuous things.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Quoting Emperor Julian and Seneca, Montaigne recommends continual labour, sobriety, and tempering bodily indulgence so the soul remains vigorous and fit for public duty and virtue.

rubrics_metrics.name: Avoid rash vows to die in battle or extreme obstinacy
rubrics_metrics.description: Resolute vows to die in battle or extreme determination to secure death are often frustrated by fortune, wounds, or imprisonment and therefore are imprudent.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Montaigne recounts Roman oaths and examples (Philistus, others) where men aimed to die honorably but were thwarted. He suggests moderation, recognizing that fate and bodily frailty limit our designs to die usefully.

rubrics_metrics.name: Use of relays and trained animals/people for rapid communication (posting)
rubrics_metrics.description: Fast communication across distances is achieved by pre-arranged relays of horses, trained birds, and running litters of men.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Historical examples: Cyrus’s relay horses; Caesar's hired-coach extremes; Tiberius's rapid travel; use of swallows and pigeons with marked messages; Peruvian human relays; Wallachian couriers who forcibly take tired horses. These are practical techniques for ensuring speed in message transmission.

rubrics_metrics.name: States sometimes use 'ill means' for a salutary end
rubrics_metrics.description: Political communities may employ harmful measures (wars, forced migrations, spectacles) to purge excesses, educate vigor, or restore balance—i.e., 'ill means employed to a good end.'
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Montaigne compares bodily humoral purgations to state actions (colonies, wars) used to relieve overpopulation or social maladies. He cites Roman practices, the Bretigny treaty, and the idea that long peace breeds luxury. He warns, however, against unjust wars taken merely for advantage and invokes moral restraint (quote from Catullus).

rubrics_metrics.name: Spectacles can cultivate courage but also brutalize the populace
rubrics_metrics.description: Roman public spectacles (gladiators etc.) trained people to contempt of danger and instilled showy courage, but they also fostered cruelty and appetite for blood.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Montaigne notes the progression from condemning criminals to employing slaves, freemen, nobles, and women in such shows; he cites Prudentius to condemn the bloodthirsty pleasure. The point is ambivalent: spectacles served social training but had deleterious moral effects.

rubrics_metrics.name: Greatness is displayed as much in giving as in taking
rubrics_metrics.description: The Romans' greatness was seen not only in conquest but in what they gave or restored; power can be expressed by leaving or granting kingdoms.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Examples: Caesar's disposal of kingdoms, Antiochus being ordered by Popilius; Augustus restoring or presenting conquered realms. The political lesson is that magnanimity and the capacity to confer or withhold honors demonstrates superior power.

rubrics_metrics.name: Do not counterfeit sickness or physical defects
rubrics_metrics.description: Feigning illness or defects (gout, one-eyedness, lameness) is dangerous because imagination or bodily inaction can produce real infirmity; fortune may take us at our word.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Anecdotes: Martial’s Caelius who feigned gout and then contracted it; Appian’s disguised one-eyed man who lost sight; Pliny’s dream-of-blindness leading to real blindness; Seneca’s fool Harpaste. Montaigne advises parents to rebuke children who feign defects and warns that adopting affectations (e.g., carrying a stick) risks actual disability.

rubrics_metrics.name: Physical features and gestures carry legal and social consequences (thumbs)
rubrics_metrics.description: Thumbs are 'master fingers' with etymological importance and social/political meaning; gestures of the thumb signified favour or disfavour; maiming thumbs had legal and military implications.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Montaigne recounts Roman practices: depressing the thumb as applause, inverting it as death, exemption from service for maimed thumbs, instances of confiscation for maliciously cutting thumbs to avoid service, and punitive removal of thumbs after naval victory. The criterion: small bodily parts can have outsized civic/legal effects.

rubrics_metrics.name: Cowardice breeds cruelty
rubrics_metrics.description: Cowardice is the mother of cruelty; malicious and inhuman fierceness often accompanies feminine weakness and a mean spirit.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Montaigne gives Alexander of Pheres as an example who was cruel yet could not bear to see tragedies on stage for fear of weeping. He notes that true valour delights only in resistance ('Nor delights in killing a bull unless he resists'), implying that cruelty without worthy resistance is a sign of moral weakness.
